abstract: ABSTRACT Phosphorus is a crucial nutrient for the normal growth and development of rice. Enhancing the efficiency of phosphorus acquisition in plants is vital for optimising soil phosphorus utilisation. The SUMO E3 ligase OsSIZ1 is an important factor for regulating plant phosphorus acquisition and starvation response in rice. However, how its activity responds to Pi‐supplied conditions remains unknown. In this study, we discovered that the mutations in OsCK2β3 , which encodes a regulatory subunit of CK2, influenced the Pi starvation response. The global level of SUMOylation was found to decrease in Osck2β3 mutants, mirroring the effects observed under Pi‐deficiency treatment. Additionally, we identified that OsCK2 can interact with and phosphorylate OsSIZ1, thereby impacting its stability. Transcriptome analysis with Ossiz1 and Osck2β3 mutants revealed that the ‘OsCK2‐OsSIZ1’ module primarily regulates defence responses by influencing the expression of genes associated with the biosynthesis of diterpenoid phytoalexins and pathogenesis‐related genes, in addition to impacting the response to phosphate starvation. Notably, the overexpression of a variant of OsSIZ1, in which the phosphorylation sites targeted by OsCK2 were mutated, enhanced phosphorus acquisition and defence responses while preserving normal growth. Consequently, we not only showed how OsSIZ1 activity responds to Pi starvation but also created a variant of OsSIZ1 that improves phosphorus acquisition efficiency and enhances resistance against multiple pathogens, all without inducing growth defects.

1
Introduction
Phosphorus is one of the mineral nutrients necessary for the normal growth and development of rice (Raghothama
1999
; Lopez‐Arredondo et al.
2014
). To ensure a stable and high rice yield, phosphorus fertilisers are extensively applied in the fields. However, due to their low utilisation rate, a significant amount of unused phosphorus fertilisers can leach into rivers, leading to pollution (Vance et al.
2003
). Additionally, phosphate rock, the primary source of phosphorus fertilisers, is projected to be depleted within 50 to 100 years at the current usage rate (Baker et al.
2015
). Therefore, enhancing phosphorus acquisition and utilisation efficiency in rice is vital for fostering efficient and sustainable agricultural practices. In response to the phosphate (Pi) deficiency, plants enhance the expression of signalling genes related to phosphorus acquisition and utilisation, thereby alleviating the growth restriction caused by phosphorus deficiency (Lopez‐Arredondo et al.
2014
; Jia et al.
2023
). Therefore, analysing the molecular regulatory network governing phosphorus uptake and utilisation in rice can provide a theoretical foundation for the genetic enhancement of phosphorus nutrient efficiency in rice cultivation.
SIZ1 (SAP and Miz 1), a SUMO E3 ligase localised to the nucleus, is an important factor in regulating plant Pi homeostasis and starvation response in plants (Miura et al.
2005
; Wang et al.
2015
). Protein SUMO modification is to covalently bind the mature SUMO protein to the substrate protein, facilitated by SUMO‐activating enzyme (E1), SUMO‐binding enzyme (E2) and SUMO ligase (E3), to regulate the stability, subcellular localisation and protein activity of the targets (Datta et al.
2018
). Mutations
AtSIZ1
in
Arabidopsis thaliana
and
OsSIZ1
in rice result in increased Pi accumulation (Miura et al.
2005
; Wang et al.
2015
). Plant SIZ1 protein has five conserved domains, namely SAP, PHD, PINIT, SP‐RING and SIM (Miura et al.
2005
). The SIM motif promotes the interaction between SUMO and SIZ1 (Park et al.
2011
; Rytz et al.
2018
). On the basis of the expression of Pi starvation‐induced (PSI) genes, previous studies have indicated that AtSIZ1 plays both positive and negative roles in regulating Pi starvation response (Miura et al.
2005
). Furthermore, Arabidopsis AtSIZ1 has the capacity to modify AtPHR1 in vitro, a key transcription factor that governs the Pi starvation response in plants, although the biological significance of this SUMO modification remains unverified (Miura et al.
2005
). Notably, the expression levels of rice
OsSIZ1
and Arabidopsis
AtSIZ1
do not change in response to Pi supplied conditions, suggesting that post‐translational modifications of SIZ1 may be the mechanism that responds to such conditions.
Protein kinase CK2 is a highly conserved serine/threonine protein kinase that is widely present in eukaryotes, which is a heterotetramer composed of two regulatory subunits, CK2β and two kinase subunits, CK2α (Riera et al.
2011
; Mulekar and Huq
2014
). The substrate specificity of CK2 is characterised by the presence of multiple acidic amino acids flanking serine or threonine residues. In plants, CK2 subunits are primarily localised in the nucleus and cytoplasm (Salinas et al.
2006
; Chen et al.
2015
; Rodiger et al.
2020
). Under Pi‐sufficient conditions, the rice OsCK2 holoenzyme, consisting of OsCK2α3 and OsCK2β3, phosphorylates OsPHT1 family proteins, which results in their retention in the endoplasmic reticulum and prevents Pi overaccumulation (Chen et al.
2015
; Yang et al.
2020
). Additionally, OsCK2 plays a role in regulating phosphorus translocation from roots to shoots in rice by phosphorylating the ubiquitin‐conjugating enzyme OsPHO2 (Wang et al.
2020
). Our phosphorylation proteomics analysis indicated that Pi deficiency caused significant alterations in the phosphorylation levels of proteins in the roots, with approximately 21.5% of these proteins predicted to be substrates of OsCK2 (Yang et al.
2019
). The interactions between OsCK2 and OsPHT1 or OsPHO2 occur within the endoplasmic reticulum (Chen et al.
2015
; Wang et al.
2020
). However, both OsCK2α3 and OsCK2β3 are also localised in the nucleus, which serves as the primary site for gene expression regulation. Consequently, it remains unclear whether OsCK2 is involved in regulating the phosphorus starvation response in rice.
Pi excess and Pi deficiency increase susceptibility and resistance to pathogen infection, respectively (Campos‐Soriano et al.
2020
). Diterpenoid phytoalexins play crucial roles in resistance against multiple pathogens. On the basis of their structures, diterpenoid phytoalexins in rice can be categorised into three major groups: phytocassanes, momilactones and oryzalexins (Valletta et al.
2023
; Bian et al.
2024
). The biosynthetic pathways of diterpenoid phytoalexins in rice have been elucidated, with geranylgeranyl diphosphate serving as the common precursor for these phytoalexins. Key synthases involved in this process include copalyl diphosphate synthase (OsCPS), kaurene synthase‐like (OsKSL), cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (OsCYP99A3) and dehydrogenase (OsMAS) (Yamamura et al.
2015
; Lu et al.
2018
; Mao et al.
2020
; Valletta et al.
2023
). Nine transcription factors have been identified to directly regulate the expressions of these genes such as OsbZIP87/79, OsbHLH5/25/26 and OsWRKY10/45/53/76 (Bian et al.
2024
; Zhou et al.
2024
; Liao et al.
2025
; Lin et al.
2025
). However, the potential role of diterpenoid phytoalexins in modulating resistance associated with Pi deficiency remains unexplored.
In this study, we found that OsCK2β3 affected Pi starvation response in rice. Additionally, we observed a reduction in global SUMOylation levels in
Osck2β3
mutants, mirroring the effects of Pi deficiency treatment. Further, we revealed that OsCK2 interacts with and phosphorylates OsSIZ1. Transcriptome analysis indicated that the ‘OsCK2‐OsSIZ1’ module plays a role in mediating rice disease resistance by regulating the expression of genes involved in the biosynthesis of diterpenoid phytoalexins. Finally, we confirmed that the overexpression of non‐phosphorylatable OsSIZ1 not only improved Pi accumulation without growth penalty, but also induced the expression of genes responsible for the biosynthesis of diterpenoid phytoalexins, thereby enhancing resistance against multiple pathogens.

Results
2.1
Mutation of
OsCK2β3
and
OsSIZ1
Led to Pi Accumulation and Changed the Pi Starvation Response
To investigate the function of OsCK2β3 in regulating Pi homeostasis and Pi starvation response, we generated
Osck2β3
mutants by CRISPR‐Cas9 technology (Figure
S1A
). After culturing these mutants in Pi‐sufficient conditions for 30 days, we observed growth defects compared to the wild type (Figure
1A
; Figure
S1C
). Pi concentrations in the shoots and roots of
Osck2β3
mutants were approximately 1.5‐fold and 2.5‐fold higher, respectively, than those in the wild type under Pi‐sufficient conditions (Figure
1B
), consistent with previous research (Chen et al.
2015
). Pi deficiency typically inhibits rice shoot growth while promoting root growth, which is a standard response to Pi starvation in rice. Under Pi‐deficient conditions, growth performance and Pi levels were comparable between
Osck2β3
mutants and the wild type (Figure
1A
). Given that OsCK2β3 can target the nucleus (Chen et al.
2015
), we speculated that CK2 plays a role in regulating the Pi starvation response. We examined several Pi starvation‐induced (PSI) genes in
Osck2β3
mutants under Pi‐sufficient conditions (Figure
1C
). While the PSI genes
OsPT2
and
OsPAP21b
were upregulated in the roots of
Osck2β3
mutants, the expression level of
OsIPS1
remained similar to that of the wild type. Although
OsPT8
is not classified as a PSI gene in rice, its expression was also induced in
Osck2β3
mutants (Figure
1C
). These findings suggest that OsCK2 also regulates the Pi starvation response, in addition to phosphorylating members of the OsPHT1 family and OsPHO2 in rice.

Our previous phosphorylation proteomics analysis revealed that phosphorylated OsSIZ1 decreased following Pi deficiency, with the identified phosphorylation site being a typical CK2 phosphorylation motif (Yang et al.
2019
). To test whether OsCK2β3 regulates the function of OsSIZ1 in rice, we first assessed the global profile of SUMOylation in
Osck2β3
mutants using a SUMO antibody. Pi deficiency resulted in a ~31% reduction in global SUMOylation levels in the wild type (Figure
1D,E
). Notably, the mutation of OsCK2β3 caused 24% to 30% decrease in global SUMOylation levels compared to those under Pi‐sufficient conditions (Figure
1D,E
). We subsequently generated
Ossiz1
mutants by CRISPR‐Cas9 to evaluate expressions of PSI genes (Figure
S1B
). After growing these mutants under Pi‐sufficient conditions for 30 days, we found that the roots and shoots of
Ossiz1
mutants were slightly smaller than those of the wild type, though remarkably, their fresh weight was significantly lower (Figure
1A
; Figure
S1C
). However, under Pi‐deficient conditions, root growth in
Ossiz1
mutants was significantly inhibited. The Pi levels in the roots and shoots of
Ossiz1
mutants were 1.5‐fold and 1.8‐fold higher, respectively, than those in the wild type (Figure
1B
), which aligns with previous research (Wang et al.
2015
). Interestingly, under Pi‐deficient conditions, Pi concentrations were similar between
Ossiz1
mutants and the wild type. Furthermore, the mutation of
OsSIZ1
also led to the upregulation of
OsPT2
,
OsPT8
and
OsPAP21b
(Figure
1C
). Pi starvation promotes the growth of root hairs in both rice and Arabidopsis (Miura et al.
2005
; Guo et al.
2015
). Subsequently, we compared the root hair growth in
Ossiz1
and
Osck2β3
mutants under conditions with or without Pi supply. When Pi is starved, the root hair density of the wild type is enhanced by about 25% and the root hair length under Pi deficiency is doubled compared to that under Pi sufficiency (Figure
S2
). Although the mutation of
OsCK2β3
does not significantly change the root hair growth under Pi‐deficient condition, the mutation of
Ossiz1
significantly enhances root hair length compared to its wild type under Pi starvation (Figure
S2
), similar to
Atsiz1
in Arabidopsis (Miura et al.
2005
).
2.2
OsCK2
Could Interact With
OsSIZ1
To explore the potential direct interaction between OsCK2 and OsSIZ1, we initially conducted a yeast two‐hybrid experiment. This involved cloning two CK2α‐coding genes,
OsCK2α2
and
OsCK2α3
, along with two CK2β‐encoding genes,
OsCK2β1
and
OsCK2β3
, into bait vectors, while inserting the
OsSIZ1
coding sequence into a prey vector. Following the co‐transformation of these vectors into AH109 yeast cells, the combination of
OsCK2β3
and
OsSIZ1
constructs exhibited growth on ‐Leu‐Trp‐His‐Ade medium, indicating that OsCK2β3 interacts with OsSIZ1 in yeast (Figure
2A
). To pinpoint the OsCK2β3‐interacting domain of OsSIZ1, we divided the OsSIZ1 protein into two segments: OsSIZ1‐N (amino acids 1–450, which includes the SAP, PHD, PINIT and SR‐RING domains, as well as the first SIM domain) and OsSIZ1‐C (amino acids 410–876, which contains the second SIM domain) (Figure
S3
). The results showed that OsCK2β3 strongly interacted with the N terminus of OsSIZ1, but not with the C terminus, in yeast. A pulldown assay further demonstrated that His‐OsSIZ1 could be pulled down by GST‐OsCK2β3, but not by GST alone, thereby confirming their interaction in vitro (Figure
2B
). To validate this interaction in plants, we expressed OsSIZ1‐Flag alongside OsCK2β3‐GFP or GFP in tobacco leaves. Following immunoprecipitation with a GFP antibody, OsSIZ1‐Flag was detected in conjunction with OsCK2β3‐GFP, but not with GFP alone (Figure
2C
). The split bimolecular fluorescence complementation assay clearly illustrated that their interaction occurred within the nucleus of the plant (Figure
2D
). Additionally, we discovered that the kinase subunit OsCK2α3 could interact with OsSIZ1, facilitated by OsCK2β3 in plants. Collectively, these findings suggest that the OsCK2 holoenzyme can interact with OsSIZ1 both in vivo and in vitro.

2.3
OsCK2
Could Phosphorylate
OsSIZ1
To investigate whether OsCK2 phosphorylates OsSIZ1, we initially predicted the potential phosphorylation sites in OsSIZ1 targeted by OsCK2 using the Group‐based Prediction System (GPS). This analysis identified 12 serine/threonine (S/T) residues as potential CK2 substrates (Figure
S4
). A kinase assay was conducted utilising Phos‐tag Biotin, which allows for the detection of phosphorylated proteins with HRP‐labelled Streptavidin. The results indicated that OsSIZ1 could be phosphorylated by the OsCK2 holoenzyme, but not by GST alone (Figure
3B
). To refine the identification of target sites, we compared the protein sequences of OsSIZ1 and AtSIZ1, revealing six conserved sites—S
348
, S
350
, S
607
, S
609
, T
873
and S
875
—as the most likely phosphorylation targets of OsCK2 (Figure
S5
). The phosphorylated band was absent when all six conserved sites were mutated to alanine (His‐OsSIZ1
6A
) (Figure
3B

Discussion
Plant CK2 subunits are predominantly localised to the nucleus and cytoplasm (Salinas et al.
2006
; Chen et al.
2015
). In rice, the OsCK2 holoenzyme, composed of OsCK2α3 and phosphorylated OsCK2β3, regulates Pi homeostasis by phosphorylating OsPHT1 family proteins and the ubiquitin‐conjugating enzyme OsPHO2. However, the interaction between OsCK2 and OsPHT1 or OsPHO2 occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (Chen et al.
2015
; Wang et al.
2020
). The nucleus serves as the primary site for gene expression regulation. Consequently, it remains unclear whether OsCK2 also influences the Pi starvation response in rice. In this study, we discovered that OsCK2 regulates gene expression primarily through OsSIZ1 in rice, generating a variant of OsSIZ1 that enhances Pi absorption and plant defence without incurring growth penalties.
Our findings indicate that OsCK2 can interact with OsSIZ1 in vitro and specifically phosphorylate OsSIZ1 at S
607
and S
609
(Figure
3
). Our phosphoproteome depends on the enrichment of phosphorylated proteins using TiO2 bulk beads, which suggests that the phosphorylation level of OsSIZ1 is diminished, even though the phosphorylation sites identified in this study were not observed (Yang et al.
2019
). The protease trypsin used in our earlier research could only digest proteins at the carboxyl side of lysine or arginine (Yang et al.
2019
), resulting in a 53‐amino acid fragment of OsSIZ1 containing S
607
and S
609
, which is outside the effective range of mass spectrometry detection. In this study, by mutating S
607
and S
609
to alanine in the kinase assay and truncating OsSIZ1 for mass spectrometry detection, we ultimately confirmed the phosphorylated sites in OsSIZ1 for OsCK2 (Figure
3
). Interestingly, PIAS1, the human homologue of OsSIZ1, can be phosphorylated by CK2 at the same SIM domain (Stehmeier and Muller
2009
), indicating a conserved regulatory pathway.
As the interaction between OsCK2 and OsSIZ1 occurs in the nucleus, gene expression modification is expected to be the outcome of this interaction. The overexpression of the non‐phosphorylatable OsSIZ1 improved Pi accumulation without growth penalties in shoot. The expression of many PSI genes could be adjusted to improve phosphorus absorption in rice; however, this process concurrently hinders plant growth (Zhou et al.
2008
; Wang et al.
2014
; Jia et al.
2017
; Xu et al.
2019
). We aimed to identify the general pathway regulated by the ‘OsCK2‐OsSIZ1’ module in shoots. Transcriptome data revealed that
OsPT2
and
OsPAP21b
were also induced in the shoots of both
Osck2β3
and
Ossiz1
mutants (Table
S1
). In roots,
OsPT8
was induced in both
Osck2β3
and
Ossiz1
mutants, while
OsIPS1
remained unchanged. This phenomenon is reminiscent of the
Atsiz1
, where the PSI genes
AtPT2
,
AtPS2
and
AtPS3
were induced, but
AtRNS1
was reduced in Arabidopsis (Miura et al.
2005
). Furthermore, the upregulation of
OsPT2
and
OsPAP21b
, but not other PSI genes such as
OsIPS1
, suggests that
OsSIZ1
may regulate Pi homeostasis through transcription factors other than OsPHR2 in rice, as OsPHR2 broadly regulates PSI genes (Zhou et al.
2008
; Wang et al.
2014
). Transcriptome analysis indicated that the majority of the induced genes in the
Osck2β3
mutant were also upregulated in the
Ossiz1
mutant. However, the induced genes accounted for only one‐quarter of the upregulated genes in the
Ossiz1
mutant (Figure
6
). Notably, most of the upregulated gene expression levels were higher in
Ossiz1
mutants than in
Osck2β3
mutants. These results suggest that OsCK2β3 regulates gene expression primarily through OsSIZ1 in rice, but OsCK2 only modifies a small portion of OsSIZ1's function.
The SIM domain promotes the binding of SUMO to human PIAS1, the homologue of OsSIZ1, as mutation of the SIM domain to a non‐phosphorylatable version (S to A) decreased its ability to bind to SUMO paralogs (Stehmeier and Muller
2009
). However, our results indicated that mutation in the SIM domain of OsSIZ1 did not alter its ability to bind to SUMO1 (Figure
S6B
), similar to the effect observed with the SIM domain mutation of AtSIZ1 in Arabidopsis (Cheong et al.
2009
). Degradation assays revealed that OsSIZ1 was more stable under Pi‐sufficient conditions. As OsCK2β3 tends to degrade after Pi starvation (Chen et al.
2015
), OsSIZ1
AA
, mimicking the non‐phosphorylatable form, exhibited a faster degradation rate than OsSIZ1, further demonstrating the role of the SIM domain in regulating OsSIZ1 stability in rice. Overexpression of
OsSIZ1
AA
induced PSI genes and genes involved in diterpenoid phytoalexin biosynthesis, similar to the effects of
OsSIZ1
mutation, suggesting that this non‐phosphorylatable OsSIZ1 seems to be a loss‐of‐function mutant. However, overexpression of
OsSIZ1
AA
enhanced global SUMOylation levels without inhibiting growth (Figures
4
and
5
), indicating that its SUMO E3 ligase activity may not be compromised by the mutation. Indeed, complementing the AtSIZ1
AA
, which involved mutating the same double serines to alanines, nearly fully restored the growth and SUMOylation levels in the Arabidopsis
Atsiz1
mutant (Cheong et al.
2009
). Previous studies have shown that the SIM domain can act as a bridge to interact with SUMOylated proteins (Lascorz et al.
2022
; Liu et al.
2023
). Thus, we speculate that the phosphorylated status of OsSIZ1 at S
607
and S
609
may also influence its interaction with certain SUMOylated proteins.
Venn analysis indicated that the majority of the induced genes in
Osck2β3
mutants were also induced in
Ossiz1
mutants, confirming that OsCK2 regulates gene expression primarily through OsSIZ1, albeit affecting only a small portion of OsSIZ1's function in rice. Pi starvation not only activates the Pi uptake system but also triggers defence responses (Campos‐Soriano et al.
2020
; He et al.
2024
). GO analysis revealed that the ‘OsCK2‐OsSIZ1’ module mainly regulates diterpene phytoalexin metabolism and defence responses in addition to the Pi starvation response in the shoot (Figure
6
). Diterpenoid phytoalexins have been widely reported to play a role in defence responses (Valletta et al.
2023
; Bian et al.
2024
). In this study, genes encoding enzymes involved in phytocassane (
OsCPS2
and
OsKSL7
), momilactone (
OsCPS4
,
OsCYP99A3
,
OsKSL4
,
OsMAS1
and
OsMAS2
) and oryzalexin (
OsKSL8
and
OsKSL10
) were induced in
Osck2β3
and
Ossiz1
mutants. These genes, along with pathogenesis‐related genes, have been shown to function in plant defence responses (Okada et al.
2009
; Yamamura et al.
2015
; Zhou et al.
2024
). Interestingly,
OsSIZ1
AA
‐Flag
lines exhibited increased resistance to
M. oryzae
,
R. solani
and
Xoo
through the induction of gene expressions involved in the biosynthesis of diterpenoid phytoalexins and pathogenesis‐related genes. Thus, the non‐phosphorylated variant of OsSIZ1 plays a dominant positive role in regulating defence responses in rice.
In summary, we found that rice OsCK2 could interact with and phosphorylate OsSIZ1 to regulate Pi starvation response, including genes involved in Pi uptake and defence response in rice (Figure
S7
). Importantly, we discovered that overexpressing the non‐phosphorylatable OsSIZ1 not only improves phosphorus absorption efficiency but also enhances defence responses against pathogens without growth deficits.

Total proteins were extracted by boiling at 95°C to 100°C for 5 min under denaturing conditions, separated by SDS‐PAGE (12% gel) and transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). Cell‐Free Degradation
For protein extraction, the shoots of WT cultivated under 0 μM and 200 Μm Pi conditions were homogenised. Then, the purified His‐tagged proteins were adjusted to equal concentrations and aliquoted into EP tubes with gradient time points (0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min, including 120 min with 10 μM MG132 protease inhibitor). Next, the reaction mixtures containing ATP (5 mM) and DTT (1 mM) were incubated at 37°C. At each time point, the samples were immediately terminated by adding SDS loading buffer, boiled at 95°C–100°C for 5 min and stored at −80°C. Finally, after all treatments, the samples were subjected to Western blotting using anti‐His antibodies to detect protein degradation patterns.
4.9
Magnaporthe oryzae
Cultivation and Infection
The Zhong 10‐8‐14 strain and experimental protocols were from Prof. Chen Xuewei's laboratory at Sichuan Agricultural University (Liao et al.
2025
). Regarding subculturing, mycelial plugs from stock cultures were transferred to PDA medium and incubated at 25°C until nearly confluent growth (about 7 days). Then, 3 mL of sterilised water was added and the mixture was pipette‐mixed to fragment the mycelia, which were then spread onto oat‐tomato agar. After 2 days of static incubation at 25°C, sterile cotton swabs were used to remove surface hyphae. Next, the plates were rinsed with sterile water, sealed with double‐layer gauze and exposed to light for 2 to 3 days to induce sporulation. Rice plants cultivated for 1 month under 5 and 200 μM Pi conditions were selected for blast resistance assessment. At 2–3 days post‐sporulation of
Magnaporthe oryzae
, 6 cm leaf segments from identical nodal positions were excised and immediately immersed in 30 mL of 10 μg/mL 6‐BA solution within 9 cm Petri dishes. Leaf surfaces were gently wounded at 1.5 cm intervals using sterile pipette tips, then returned to the 6‐BA solution. Fungal plates were hydrated with 4–5 mL sterile water and hyphae were fragmented using pipette tips to collect spore suspensions. Spore concentration was quantified via haemocytometer under microscopy and adjusted to 3–4 × 10
5
spores/mL. Each wounded leaf received 5 μL spore suspension at three sites (with resuspension between applications). After 12 h of dark incubation at 25°C, samples were transferred to light conditions (25°C, 14 h/10 h photoperiod) for 7 days for symptom development, followed by photographic documentation and calculation of the average lesion length (mm) of ≥ 21 individual lesions as the resistance index.
4.10
Rhizoctonia solani
Cultivation and Infection
Rice plants were cultivated for 30 days under 5 and 200 μM Pi conditions. Subsequently, fully expanded leaves with excised tips were detached and placed on water‐saturated filter papers in trays. Additional moistened filter papers were used to cover both leaf termini to prevent desiccation. The
R. solani
strain AG‐1 IA was inoculated onto potato–sucrose–agar medium at 28°C for 48 h until complete mycelial colonisation. 5‐mm‐diameter mycelial plugs were aseptically excised from the colonised plates and placed adaxially on the leaf surfaces. Lesion development was monitored until appropriate symptoms. Then, photographs were taken and the length of the lesion was measured (Wang et al.
2025
).

Rice plants were cultivated for 30 days under 5 and 200 μM Pi conditions.
Xoo
